metrics.title: Inflation
metrics.question: Is inflation back to the Bank of England's 2% target?

headline.caption: annual CPI inflation, measured over the past 12 months

context: Prices overall are 7.1% higher than in June 2024, the last full month before the general election.
Inflation was 2.0% in June 2024 and is 3.1% now. The target is 2%.
Falling inflation does not mean prices fall. It means they rise more slowly.

sources.title: Consumer price inflation, UK
series: CPI annual rate and CPI index, all items (D7G7, D7BT)

metrics.method: The Consumer Prices Index annual rate published by the ONS, and the CPI index level used for the change since June 2024.

explainer.what: Inflation is how fast prices are rising. The figure is the change in the Consumer Prices Index over the past 12 months.
explainer.why: The Bank of England is required to keep inflation at 2%. When pay rises more slowly than prices, households are worse off even though wages are going up.

metrics.title: Real wages
metrics.question: Is pay keeping up with prices?

headline.caption: change in real regular pay since the election (now £531 a week)

context: Average regular pay is worth £531 a week after inflation, against £523 in June 2024.
The highest this measure has ever reached is £535 a week, in Mar 2026.
Real pay is what your wage actually buys once prices are taken into account.

chart.note: Average weekly regular pay in Great Britain, adjusted for inflation and seasonally adjusted, set to 100 in June 2024.

sources.title: Average weekly earnings in Great Britain
series: AWE whole economy, real terms level, regular pay, seasonally adjusted (A3WX)

metrics.method: ONS Average Weekly Earnings, whole economy regular pay (excluding bonuses), in real terms and seasonally adjusted, indexed to June 2024.

explainer.what: Average weekly earnings adjusted for inflation, so the figures can be compared over time.
explainer.why: This is the clearest measure of whether working people are better or worse off than they were.

metrics.title: 1.5 million new homes
metrics.question: Is England on course for 1.5 million new homes this parliament?

headline.caption: homes added to England's housing stock in the latest full financial year

context: The pledge counts net additional dwellings: new builds, plus conversions and changes of use, minus demolitions.
208,600 homes were added in 2024–25, fewer than the year before.
Reaching 1.5 million over a five-year parliament needs about 300,000 a year, roughly half as much again as the latest figure.
Housing is devolved, so the target covers England only.

On 13 September 2026 the Housing Secretary, Angela Rayner, said there was a “slim chance” of hitting the target but that she was “definitely not giving it up”, blaming construction costs and international headwinds.

chart.note: Net additional dwellings in England, financial years. The 2024–25 figure covers a few months of the previous government.

sources.publisher: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
sources.title: Housing supply: net additional dwellings, England
series: Net additional dwellings, England, 2024-25

sources.title: Is the government on track to deliver 1.5 million new homes?

metrics.method: Net additional dwellings in England, as published by MHCLG and compiled by Full Fact's government tracker. The pace needed is 1.5 million divided across the five years of a parliament.

explainer.what: The number of homes added to England's housing stock in a year, counting conversions and demolitions as well as new builds.
explainer.why: Housing supply is the main lever on housing costs over time, and 1.5 million homes was one of the government's six headline milestones.

metrics.title: Unemployment
metrics.question: Are more people out of work than when the government took office?

headline.caption: unemployment rate, people aged 16 and over

context: The unemployment rate was 4.2% at the general election and is 4.9% now.
The employment rate for people aged 16 to 64 is 75.1%, against 74.7% in June 2024.
20.9% of people aged 16 to 64 are economically inactive: neither working nor looking for work.

sources.title: Labour market overview, UK
series: Unemployment rate, employment rate and inactivity rate, seasonally adjusted (MGSX, LF24, LF2S)

metrics.method: ONS Labour Force Survey, seasonally adjusted, published in the monthly labour market overview. The ONS has warned that survey response rates make these estimates less reliable than usual.

explainer.what: The share of people in the labour force who are out of work and looking for a job.
explainer.why: It is the clearest measure of whether the jobs market is getting easier or harder, though it misses people who have stopped looking.

metrics.title: GDP per person vs total GDP
metrics.question: Is the economy growing for each person, or only because the population is growing?

headline.caption: change in GDP per person since the election, while total GDP grew +2.1%

context: Since the general election the economy as a whole has grown +2.1%, while output per person has changed by +1.7%.
The gap is population growth of about 0.5% over the same period.
GDP per person was £10,196 in Jan–Mar 2026, against £10,030 in the quarter of the election.

chart.note: Real (inflation-adjusted) GDP and GDP per person, seasonally adjusted, each set to 100 in the quarter of the general election. Where the total line rises faster than the per-person line, the difference is population growth.

sources.title: GDP quarterly national accounts, UK
series: Gross domestic product and GDP per head, chained volume measures, seasonally adjusted (ABMI, IHXW)

metrics.method: ONS quarterly national accounts: real GDP (ABMI) and real GDP per head (IHXW), both chained volume measures and seasonally adjusted, each indexed to the June quarter of 2024.

explainer.what: GDP is everything the economy produces. GDP per person divides that by the population.
explainer.why: Total GDP can grow simply because there are more people. GDP per person is the better guide to living standards.

metrics.title: Productivity
metrics.question: Is the country producing more for each hour worked?

headline.caption: change in output per hour worked since the election

context: Productivity is output per hour worked. Over the long run it is what allows pay to rise without prices rising.
Output per hour is +0.3% compared with the quarter of the general election.

sources.title: Labour productivity, UK
series: UK whole economy output per hour worked, seasonally adjusted (LZVB)

metrics.method: ONS labour productivity: whole economy output per hour worked, seasonally adjusted, indexed to the June quarter of 2024.

explainer.what: How much the economy produces for each hour of work.
explainer.why: Sustained pay rises and better public services ultimately depend on producing more per hour. UK productivity has grown slowly since the financial crisis.

metrics.title: Interest rates
metrics.question: What is it costing to borrow, and who decides?

headline.caption: Bank Rate, set by the Bank of England

context: Bank Rate was 5.25% at the general election and is 3.75% now.
A typical two-year fixed mortgage at 75% loan-to-value is 4.92%, and the average standard variable rate is 6.58%.
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee sets Bank Rate independently of ministers, to meet the 2% inflation target.

sources.title: Bank of England official Bank Rate and quoted household interest rates
series: IUMABEDR
IUMBV34
IUMTLMV

metrics.method: Bank of England statistical database: official Bank Rate (IUMABEDR), the quoted rate on a two-year fixed mortgage at 75% loan-to-value (IUMBV34) and the average standard variable rate (IUMTLMV), monthly.

explainer.what: Bank Rate is the interest rate the Bank of England pays commercial banks, and it feeds through to mortgages, loans and savings.
explainer.why: It is the main tool for controlling inflation, and it decides what mortgages cost. The government does not set it.

metrics.title: Government borrowing
metrics.question: How much more is the government spending than it raises?

headline.caption: public sector net borrowing over the past 12 months

context: Over the 12 months to Jul 2026 the government borrowed £123.8 billion.
Borrowing is the yearly gap between what the state spends and what it raises. Debt is the running total of every past gap.
In the latest month alone, the government borrowed £1.8 billion.

chart.note: Public sector net borrowing excluding public sector banks, by month. Positive bars are months when the government borrowed; bars below the line are surpluses, usually January and July when self-assessment tax arrives.

sources.title: Public sector finances, UK
series: Public sector net borrowing excluding public sector banks, £ million (J5II)

metrics.method: ONS public sector finances: net borrowing excluding public sector banks. The headline is the sum of the latest 12 months.

explainer.what: The difference between what the government spends and what it raises in tax, in one period.
explainer.why: Every pound borrowed is added to the national debt and has to be serviced out of future taxes.

metrics.title: Government debt
metrics.question: How much does the state owe, measured against the size of the economy?

headline.caption: public sector net debt as a share of GDP

context: Debt was 94.5% of the economy at the general election and is 94.1% now.
Debt as a share of GDP is the measure the government's own fiscal rules use, because it compares what is owed with the size of the economy that has to service it.

series.name: Public sector net debt, % of GDP

sources.title: Public sector finances, UK
series: Public sector net debt excluding public sector banks, as a share of GDP (HF6X)

metrics.method: ONS public sector finances: net debt excluding public sector banks, as a percentage of GDP, published monthly.

explainer.what: Everything the state owes, minus its liquid assets, measured against the size of the economy.
explainer.why: Interest on this debt is paid before anything else. The larger it is relative to the economy, the more of each year's taxes go to servicing it.

metrics.title: NHS 18-week waits
metrics.question: Are NHS patients in England being treated within 18 weeks?

headline.caption: of patients waiting less than 18 weeks for planned treatment

context: The standard is that 92% of patients should wait no more than 18 weeks from referral to treatment. It has not been met since 2015.
65.8% of patients were within 18 weeks at the end of June 2026.
The government set an interim goal of 65% by March 2026, which it met.
The waiting list covers England. Health is devolved elsewhere in the UK.

chart.note: Share of patients on the referral-to-treatment waiting list who have been waiting less than 18 weeks, England.

sources.title: Referral to treatment waiting times statistics, June 2026
Is the government on course to meet the NHS 18-week standard?

metrics.method: NHS England referral-to-treatment statistics: the percentage of incomplete pathways waiting under 18 weeks, as published monthly and compiled by Full Fact's government tracker.

explainer.what: The share of people waiting for planned hospital treatment in England who have waited less than 18 weeks since being referred.
explainer.why: It is the official measure of hospital waiting times and the one the government chose for its own milestone.

metrics.title: Net migration
metrics.question: How many more people are arriving to live in the UK than leaving?

headline.caption: net long-term international migration

context: Net migration was 171,000 in the year to Dec 2025, against 649,000 in the year to the election.
The peak was 944,000 in the year to Mar 2023, before the election.
That net figure is the difference between two much larger flows: 813,000 people arrived and 642,000 left.
Of the latest net figure, 350,000 were non-EU nationals.
These are provisional estimates, described by the ONS as official statistics in development, and they are revised as more data arrives. Earlier figures have moved by tens of thousands.

chart.note: ONS long-term international migration, rolling year-ending estimates. Net migration is immigration minus emigration.

sources.title: Long-term international immigration, emigration and net migration flows, provisional
series: Long-term international migration by flow and nationality (table 1)

metrics.method: ONS long-term international migration, provisional estimates, table 1: year-ending estimates of immigration, emigration and net migration for the UK. Official statistics in development, revised as administrative data matures.

explainer.what: The number of people arriving to live in the UK for at least a year, minus the number leaving.
explainer.why: It drives population growth, and it is the number the whole immigration argument is conducted in. It is an estimate, not a count, and it is revised.

metrics.title: Returns and removals
metrics.question: How many people with no right to be in the UK are actually leaving?

headline.caption: people returned from the UK over the past 12 months

context: 40,605 people were returned in the 12 months to Jun 2026, against 31,152 in the 12 months to the election: a change of +30.3%.
Of those, 9,669 were enforced returns and 30,936 were voluntary. Enforced returns are much the smaller share, and the one ministers are usually asked about.

A further 18,646 people were refused entry at the border and subsequently left. The Home Office counts these separately and they are not in the headline figure, which is why totals quoted elsewhere are sometimes much higher.
A return is not the same as a deportation, which is a specific power used mainly after a criminal conviction.

chart.note: Home Office returns data (table Ret_D02), as rolling four-quarter totals so the seasonal pattern does not distort the trend. 'All returns' is the Home Office headline measure: enforced plus voluntary. People refused entry at the border are shown separately and are not included in it.

sources.title: Immigration system statistics: returns from the UK (Ret_D02)
series: Returns from the UK by return destination and return type (Ret_D02)

metrics.method: Home Office quarterly returns dataset Ret_D02, summed across destinations into rolling four-quarter totals. The headline follows the Home Office's own definition of a return: enforced returns plus voluntary returns. People refused entry at the border who subsequently departed are a separate published category and are charted separately rather than added in.

explainer.what: The number of people leaving the UK who had no right to remain, whether removed by the Home Office or leaving voluntarily.
explainer.why: Arrivals get the attention, but a system's credibility rests on whether people refused permission to stay actually leave. Governments of both parties are judged on this figure.

metrics.title: Small boat arrivals
metrics.question: How many people are crossing the Channel in small boats each month?

headline.caption: people detected arriving in small boats over the past 12 months

context: 28,982 people arrived in the 12 months to Aug 2026, compared with 44,767 in the 12 months before that.
About 81,312 people have arrived since the general election in July 2024.
The busiest month on record in this series is Aug 2022, with 8,631 arrivals.
In the latest complete month, Aug 2026, there were 2,313 arrivals.
Arrivals are highly seasonal: crossings peak in summer when the Channel is calmest, so months should be compared with the same month a year earlier.

series.name: People arriving in small boats, by month

chart.note: Home Office and Border Force daily figures, added up by calendar month. The current, incomplete month is left out. These are people detected arriving; they are not the whole of irregular migration.

sources.title: Small boat activity in the English Channel (transparency data)
series: Migrants detected crossing the English Channel in small boats — daily time series (SB_01)

metrics.method: Home Office transparency data: daily counts of people detected arriving in the UK in small boats, summed by calendar month. The series begins in 2018 and is updated weekly. The incomplete current month is excluded. These figures count arrivals detected by Border Force, and are not the same as asylum claims or as total irregular migration.

explainer.what: The number of people detected crossing the English Channel in small boats and arriving in the UK.
explainer.why: It is the most visible measure of control of the border, and the figure most often cited in the debate about asylum. It is published weekly, so it is unusually current.

metrics.title: Clean power by 2030
metrics.question: How much of Britain's electricity is now low-carbon?

headline.caption: of Great Britain's electricity from clean sources

context: ‘Clean power’ is the government’s own definition: generation from nuclear and renewables, in Great Britain, excluding energy from waste and combined heat and power.
The share fell in 2025, from a revised 73.7% to 73.3%. DESNZ attributes the fall to a lower nuclear share and more gas generation covering a drop in imported electricity.
That is a fall in the first full calendar year of this government, against a commitment to reach at least 95% by 2030.
The 2024 figure was first published as 73.8% and has since been revised to 73.7%.
There is no 2026 figure on this definition: DESNZ publishes the metric once a year, and 2026 data is due in March 2027.

In September 2026 the National Audit Office found that delivering the grid upgrades the target depends on by 2030 ‘will be very challenging’, and that none of the projects the system operator flagged for acceleration had been significantly accelerated.
Electricity generation is measured for Great Britain; Northern Ireland is part of a separate grid.

chart.note: Share of Great Britain's electricity generation from clean sources on the government's Clean Power 2030 definition (DESNZ metric 1b).

sources.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
sources.title: Clean Power 2030 metrics (2025 data published 2 April 2026)

sources.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
sources.title: Annual Report and Accounts 2025 to 2026: performance report

sources.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
sources.title: Clean Power 2030 Action Plan
Upgrading the electricity transmission network

metrics.method: DESNZ Clean Power 2030 metric 1b: clean generation as a share of all Great Britain generation, where clean is nuclear plus renewables, excluding energy from waste and combined heat and power. Published once a year as accredited official statistics. Not comparable with the Energy Trends low-carbon share, which covers the whole UK and uses a wider definition.

explainer.what: The proportion of the electricity Britain generates that comes from renewables and nuclear rather than gas and coal.
explainer.why: It decides how exposed household bills are to world gas prices, and it is the government's central energy commitment.

metrics.title: 13,000 neighbourhood police
metrics.question: Are there more police in neighbourhood roles?

headline.caption: additional officers, PCSOs and special constables in neighbourhood roles

benchmark.label: The commitment
benchmark.text: 13,000 by the end of the parliament

context: The milestone counts police officers, police community support officers and special constables working in neighbourhood roles in England and Wales.
3,123 more were in post by 28 February 2026, about a quarter of the 13,000 promised.
That was ahead of the government's own first-year goal of 2,972.
The figures are Home Office management information, not accredited official statistics, and the baseline is March 2025 rather than the election.

chart.note: Additional officers, PCSOs and special constables in neighbourhood roles, England and Wales, against a baseline of 31 March 2025.

sources.title: Neighbourhood policing guarantee
series: Neighbourhood policing management information

sources.title: Is the government on track for 13,000 neighbourhood police?

metrics.method: Home Office management information on neighbourhood policing numbers, as compiled by Full Fact's government tracker, measured against the 31 March 2025 baseline the government itself uses.

explainer.what: Extra police officers, PCSOs and special constables assigned to neighbourhood policing teams.
explainer.why: Visible local policing is what most people mean by 'police on the beat', and the government set a specific number.

metrics.title: Asylum backlog
metrics.question: How many people are waiting for a first decision on an asylum claim?

headline.caption: people awaiting an initial decision on an asylum claim

context: 40,168 people were waiting for a first decision at Apr–Jun 2026, against 118,882 at the election: -66.2%.
The highest figure in this series is 175,457, in Apr–Jun 2023, under the previous government.
The backlog and hotel use move together: people waiting on a decision are the people who need accommodation, so deciding claims faster is the main way hotel numbers come down.
This counts claims awaiting an initial Home Office decision. It does not count appeals, which are heard by the courts and have a backlog of their own.

chart.note: Home Office quarterly asylum data (table Asy_D03), people awaiting an initial decision at the end of each quarter.

sources.title: Immigration system statistics: asylum claims awaiting a decision (Asy_D03)
series: Asylum claims awaiting an initial decision or further review (Asy_D03)

metrics.method: Home Office quarterly dataset Asy_D03: people with a claim awaiting an initial decision at the end of each quarter, summed across nationalities. The published bulletin also reports a lower figure counting cases rather than people, because one case can cover a family.

explainer.what: The number of people who have claimed asylum and are still waiting to be told whether they can stay.
explainer.why: Almost everything else follows from it. People waiting are people the state houses and supports, so the backlog drives the cost, the hotels and the local tension around them.

metrics.title: Asylum seekers in hotels
metrics.question: How many people claiming asylum are being housed in hotels?

headline.caption: asylum seekers in hotel accommodation

context: 16,021 people supported by the Home Office were living in hotels at Apr–Jun 2026, against 29,561 at the election.
The number rose after the election before falling, peaking at 38,054 in Oct–Dec 2024.
The highest figure in this series is 56,018, in Jul–Sep 2023, under the previous government.
Hotels housed 17% of the 93,293 asylum seekers receiving Home Office support at that date; the rest are in dispersal or initial accommodation, or receive money only.
Hotel use is the most visible and most contested part of asylum accommodation, and has been the focus of local protests.
The accommodation breakdown starts at the end of 2022. Earlier support figures exist but do not separate hotels the same way.

chart.note: Home Office quarterly asylum support data (table Asy_D09), counting people in contingency hotel accommodation at the end of each quarter.

sources.title: Immigration system statistics: asylum seekers in receipt of support (Asy_D09)
series: Asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support, by accommodation type (Asy_D09)

metrics.method: Home Office quarterly asylum support dataset Asy_D09. People recorded in 'Contingency Accommodation - Hotel' at the end of each quarter, summed across nationalities and UK regions. Published quarterly, roughly two months after the quarter ends.

explainer.what: The number of people waiting on an asylum claim who are being housed in hotels at public expense.
explainer.why: Hotels are the most visible form of asylum accommodation, the most expensive per person, and the focus of local protest. Both the government and its critics use this figure, so it is worth seeing in full.

metrics.title: Do communities get on?
metrics.question: Do people think their area is one where different backgrounds get on well together?

headline.caption: agree their local area is a place where people from different backgrounds get on well together

context: 78.5% agreed in 2025–26, against 81.4% in 2023–24, the last full year before the election.
The fall in the latest year, 80.6% to 78.5%, is the sharpest of the three.
This is the government's own headline measure of community cohesion, asked of more than 175,000 people in England.

The Community Life Survey was replaced by the Community and Engagement Survey during this period. The overlapping year is identical in both, so the series is comparable, but the question is now asked over October to March rather than across a full year.
It measures what people say about their own area, which is consistently more positive than what they say about the country.

series.name: Agree people from different backgrounds get on well together

chart.note: England, adults aged 16 and over. Community Life Survey to 2024–25, Community and Engagement Survey from 2025–26.

sources.publisher: Department for Culture, Media and Sport
sources.title: Community and Engagement Survey 2025/26: neighbourhood (table D13)
series: Extent of agreement that your local area is a place where people from different backgrounds get on well together

sources.publisher: Department for Culture, Media and Sport
sources.title: Community Life Survey 2024/25 annual publication (table B6a)
series: Extent of agreement that your local area is a place where people from different backgrounds get on well together

metrics.method: Share of adults in England answering 'definitely agree' or 'tend to agree' that their local area is a place where people from different backgrounds get on well together. Taken from the Community and Engagement Survey for 2025–26 and the Community Life Survey for earlier years; each release publishes its own year and the one before it, and the overlapping year matches.

explainer.what: How many people say the place they live is one where people from different backgrounds get on well together.
explainer.why: It is the closest thing the government has to a direct measure of whether communities are holding together, and it is asked the same way every year of a very large sample.

metrics.title: Hate crime
metrics.question: How many crimes are recorded as motivated by hostility to who someone is?

headline.caption: hate crimes recorded by the police, excluding the Metropolitan Police

context: 115,990 hate crimes were recorded in 2024–25, against 113,166 the year before: +2.5%.
Race is the largest strand, at 82,490 offences.

The Metropolitan Police is left out of every year shown. It changed crime recording system in 2024–25, so its figures are no longer comparable, and the Home Office excludes them from its own trend table. Including them would show a fall that is an artefact of the system change.

A hate crime is any offence the victim or anyone else perceives as motivated by hostility to race, religion, sexual orientation, disability or transgender identity. It is recorded on perception, before any court tests it.
The long rise from 2012 onwards is partly better recording rather than more offences, so short comparisons are safer than long ones.
The year runs April to March, so the latest year covers the first nine months of this government and the three before it.

chart.note: Police recorded hate crime, England and Wales, excluding the Metropolitan Police. 2019–20 is missing because Greater Manchester Police could not supply data that year.

sources.title: Hate crime, England and Wales (bulletin table 2a)
series: Number of hate crimes recorded by the police, by monitored strand (table 2a)

metrics.method: Home Office hate crime statistics, bulletin table 2a: offences recorded by the police in England and Wales excluding the Metropolitan Police, year ending March. The Met is excluded throughout because its 2024–25 figures are not comparable with earlier years after a change of recording system. Published annually, each October.

explainer.what: Crimes the police recorded as motivated by hostility to someone's race, religion, sexual orientation, disability or transgender identity.
explainer.why: It is the closest thing to a running measure of hostility between groups. It is a record of what is reported and recorded, not of everything that happens, and recording practice has changed a lot over the years.

metrics.title: Trust in government
metrics.question: How many people say they trust the UK government?

headline.caption: of adults say they tend to trust the UK government

context: 25.1% said they tend to trust the UK government in the survey ending 28 Jun 2026, against 21.2% in the last reading before the election.
Trust rose after the election, reaching 29.2% in 30 Mar 2026, and has since fallen back.
Roughly three quarters of adults do not say they trust the government. That has been true throughout this series, under both governments.
The Opinions and Lifestyle Survey runs in irregular windows rather than on fixed dates, so the points are not evenly spaced.
An older ONS survey put trust in government at 27% in late 2023, but it asked a different sample in a different way and the two are not comparable.

series.name: Tend to trust the UK government

chart.note: ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey, Great Britain, adults aged 16 and over. Plotted at the end of each fieldwork window.

sources.title: Beyond GDP insights: UK headline measures of national well-being
series: People who tend to trust the UK government (worksheet 6)

metrics.method: ONS Beyond GDP headline measures, worksheet 6: the share of adults in Great Britain who say they tend to trust the UK government, from the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey. Each figure is plotted at the end of its fieldwork window. Published quarterly.

explainer.what: The share of adults who say they tend to trust the UK government.
explainer.why: Trust is what lets a government act. It is also the measure most likely to move on events rather than policy, so it is worth watching over years rather than between readings.

metrics.title: Children ready for school
metrics.question: Are more five-year-olds starting school ready to learn?

headline.caption: of five-year-olds reaching a good level of development

context: The measure is the share of children reaching a 'good level of development' in the Early Years Foundation Stage Profile, assessed by teachers at the end of reception.
68.3% reached that standard in 2024–25.
The milestone is 75% by 2028, which would be a record.
The assessment covers England only.

chart.note: Share of children reaching a good level of development at the end of reception, England.

sources.title: Early years foundation stage profile results
series: Good level of development, England

sources.title: Is the government on track for 75% of children ready to learn?

metrics.method: Department for Education Early Years Foundation Stage Profile results: the percentage of children achieving a good level of development, as compiled by Full Fact's government tracker.

explainer.what: Teachers assess every child at the end of reception across communication, physical development, literacy, maths and personal development.
explainer.why: Children who start school behind tend to stay behind, so this is an early indicator of how the school system will perform for years afterwards.
